t: Queens That Can Attack the King — Editorial
o:
## Understanding the problem

We have an 8x8 board with one king and several queens. A queen attacks the king if she lies on the same row, column, or diagonal **with no other queen between them** (queens block each other). We must return all queens that can directly attack the king.

**Example 1:** king at (0,0). Queen (0,1) shares row 0 with nothing in between → attacks. Queen (1,0) shares column 0 → attacks. Queen (3,3) is on the main diagonal with no queen in between → attacks. Queens (4,0), (0,4) are blocked by (1,0) and (0,1); (2,4) shares no line → excluded.

**Example 2:** king at (3,3). Queen (2,2) is on the diagonal one step away → attacks. Queens (3,4) and (4,4) attack via row/diagonal. Queen (1,1) is on the same diagonal but blocked by (2,2); (3,5) blocked by (3,4); (4,5) not aligned.

**Constraints:** fewer than 64 queens on a fixed 8x8 board means any reasonable simulation is fast; correctness hinges on handling blocking correctly.
k: A queen attacks the king iff she is the FIRST queen encountered when walking from the king along her shared row/column/diagonal.
There are only 8 directions to scan from the king, so scanning outward per direction gives an O(64·8) solution independent of queen count.
Blocking matters: a closer queen on the same line hides farther ones.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force — check every queen's line of sight
a.i: For each queen, determine whether she shares a row, column, or diagonal with the king. If yes, walk cell-by-cell from the queen toward the king; if no other queen occupies an intermediate cell, this queen attacks the king. With < 64 queens and ≤ 7 steps per check, this is trivially fast and very intuitive.
s: Put all queen positions into a hash set for O(1) lookup.
For each queen, test alignment: dx == 0, dy == 0, or |dx| == |dy| relative to the king.
If aligned, step from the queen toward the king one cell at a time.
If any intermediate cell contains another queen, skip this queen (blocked).
Otherwise add the queen to the answer list.
a.t: O(Q · 8) where Q < 64 — for each queen we walk at most 7 cells toward the king.
a.sp: O(Q) for the hash set of queen positions.

a.n: Approach 2: Optimal — scan 8 rays outward from the king
a.i: Instead of checking each queen, invert the direction of reasoning: from the king, walk along each of the 8 directions until you hit the first queen or leave the board. That first queen (if any) is exactly the attacker in that direction, since any other queen behind it would be blocked. This does at most 8 × 7 cell visits regardless of how many queens there are.
s: Place all queens into a set keyed by encoded coordinates.
Enumerate the 8 direction vectors (dr, dc) with components in {-1, 0, 1}, excluding (0,0).
From the king, repeatedly move one step in the current direction while staying on the board.
The first cell containing a queen is an attacker — record it and stop scanning that direction.
a.t: O(64) — at most 8 directions × 7 steps of constant work, independent of queen count.
a.sp: O(1) extra — a fixed 8×8 boolean grid (or O(Q) with a hash set).

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, start with Approach 1 to show correct handling of alignment and blocking, then offer Approach 2 as the cleaner optimal solution — it naturally encodes "nearest attacker per direction" without special-casing blockers. Common pitfalls: forgetting that diagonals require |dx| == |dy| (not just dx == dy), mishandling zero deltas when computing step signs, and forgetting that a nearer queen blocks farther ones on the same line. Edge cases: king on the board border (some directions exit immediately), a single queen, and multiple queens stacked along one ray. Follow-ups might ask for the answer on an N×N board (same algorithms scale fine) or to return the attacking distance as well.
